title: The bed stops flowering by itself — is that a problem worth a new plant?
question: A pollinator eats flowers. By frame 40,000 this bed has 8 flowers left with ants in it and 3 with none. Is a plant that keeps flowering worth building before the pollinator, or is a bed that flowers once and finishes the bed you want?
context_md:
Both columns are the same bed (your mix plus four scramblers), same seed, three stops: **frame 6,000 / 20,000 / 40,000**, top to bottom. The only difference is that the right-hand column has **no colony at all**.

The reason for the pair: the obvious reading of the left column alone is *the ants ate the flowers*. The right column says otherwise — **fewer flowers stand with no animals in the box**. Herb and scrambler both finish on purpose: an axis ends in a flower and stops, and the growing tip is used up doing it.

Already measured, so you do not have to judge it: plants are **not** dying (633 to 909 with no colony), the ants **do** eat the fallen fruit (26 standing at 40,000 with no ants, 7 with), and the thicket is worth about **four times the flowers** of the bed without it at frame 6,000.

What I want your eye on is only this: whether a bed that is bare of flowers for most of a session is a bed you mind. If it is, the pollinator needs a flowering plant that does not terminate, and that is a plant-line job before this lane's.

items.label: no colony at all
